title: Etta and Wobble's Wobbly Rescue
markdown:
Oakhaven was usually as calm as a cat napping in a sunbeam: tiny cottages, neat green gardens, a baker with flour on his nose, and the happy slightly bossy quack of ducks. Mighty oaks gave the town its name. At its heart a little duck pond sparkled like a dropped sapphire, water so clear you could almost see pebbles winking from the bottom.

Mayor Acornby was a very important fellow with a belly that jiggled when he laughed and a rather wobbly hat. But the ones who made Oakhaven truly sparkle were Etta the squirrel and Wobble the jelly robot.

Etta’s tail was practically a fluffy mark that bounced when she hopped. She could scamper up the tallest oak faster than you could say acorn pie, eyes like shiny buttons, ready to spot a fallen seed from ages away. Clever paws, always twitching, ready to untangle a knot. She loved little mysteries.

Wobble was a friendly blob of shimmering bouncy jelly, translucent and jiggly, like a giant gumdrop that could move. Two bright curious lights for eyes. He could wiggle, wobble, and float. When he moved he made a little plink, like droplets on a sunny pane, and often left a faint scent of raspberry jelly.

One sparkling morning Mayor Acornby polished his most treasured possession: the Golden Acorn Medal, shiny gold with a tiny acorn carved in the middle, Oakhaven’s award for being helpful, kind, or sometimes for having the biggest smile. “To the duck pond for fresh air and picnic snacks,” he boomed. Etta and Wobble trotted along, tails and jelly vibrating for treats.

The annual Oakhaven Picnic was the best day of the summer. The meadow by the duck pond was a riot of colour, with red-and-white checkered blankets spread everywhere. There were dandelion salads, juicy berry tarts that looked like little purple jewels, and the best fluffiest cloud-shaped muffins you ever did see, sprinkled with edible glitter. A duck stole a crust and pretended it had always belonged to her. Mayor Acornby, looking very grand, stood by the pond, chest puffed out, ready to show off his magnificent medal. “Behold,” he cried, holding it high so all could see its golden gleam.

Then whoosh. A tiny puff of wind, no bigger than a butterfly’s flutter, tickled his nose with freshly baked bread. He sneezed a mighty achoo. The medal, slick with proud polish, slipped. Down it tumbled, plink-plonk, a tiny golden rain, right into the middle of the murky duck pond.

The Mayor’s tummy did a little deflate-wobble. Happy quacks turned worried. Etta peered into the water: waving green reeds, smooth grey pebbles, a lost slightly muddy button. No shiny golden acorn. Her tail drooped a tiny bit. She had never seen the Mayor so sad.

Wobble, sitting at the edge watching a ladybug, had gone splosh when the medal went in. He had not sunk like a stone. He hovered. His jelly body, light and airy, rose to the surface and bobbed gently, ripples spreading like a cheerful smile. He looked quite pleased with himself, a perfectly round bobbing island of jelly, and he made a soft wobble-wobble as if to say, Look at me. I float. Isn’t floating fun?

Etta looked at Wobble, her clever squirrel brain whirring. She looked at the murky pond, where the medal was surely hiding. She looked back at Wobble, who was now gently bumping a bright pink lily pad, making it dance. Why did he float so well? Because he was light for his size. A tiny spark, like a firefly on a summer night, lit in her clever brain.

“Wobble,” she chirped, tail a hopeful twitch. “Can you move towards the middle, very slowly? Towards where I saw something shiny fall?”

Wobble, delighted to have a task that involved wiggling, gave a happy plink and jiggled out with purpose. Etta scampered to the edge, eyes glued, nose twitching. “That’s it. Keep going. Now, can you try to push that bit of shiny stuff? The glinty thing?”

With a determined wiggle, Wobble nudged the Golden Acorn Medal, which had settled near the muddy bottom looking rather sad. It moved. A tiny shift closer to the bank. Mayor Acornby gasped, hand flying to his wobbly hat.

“Gently, Wobble, gently,” Etta whispered. “You’re doing it. You’re like a little jelly boat with a very important mission.”

With Etta’s careful instructions, whispered like secrets on the breeze, Wobble nudged and jiggled, inch by painstaking inch. The medal, once lost in the green gloom, was now glinting closer and closer to the edge where Etta waited, paws ready, heart thumping. A reed tried to be in the way and thought better of it. Wobble made one final gentle push, a little wiggle of pure jelly determination, and there it was. Right by the grassy bank, catching the sunlight. A duck came to supervise, then left, having important quacking to do.

Etta snatched it with a lightning-fast swoop. She scampered onto the bank, shook off droplets that sparkled like tiny diamonds on her fur, and held it up, dripping but safe, a triumphant glint in her button eyes.

“Hooray,” shouted Mayor Acornby, belly wobbling with relief this time, a happy joyful jiggle. “Etta, you found it. My precious medal. And Wobble. You helped. You wonderful wobbly fellow.”

Etta placed the medal back in his hand, then turned to Wobble, who shimmered with pride. “You float so well because you’re light for your size. That medal sank because it’s heavy for its size.” She did not make a speech of it. She only flicked her tail straight again.

Wobble gave a happy wobble-wobble-plink, a sound that clearly meant he was glad he could help. He had floated and nudged, and together with Etta’s cleverness they had saved the medal. Mayor Acornby, medal safely tucked in a velvet pouch, offered them the very first cloud-shaped muffin, which Wobble nibbled with a contented squish. They sat by the pond, the sunshine warming fur and jelly. Ducks went back to being slightly bossy. A checkered blanket still held one muffin crumb that Wobble was pretending not to see, and then seeing very thoroughly. The water, which had taken the gold and given it back, winked at the pebbles as if nothing at all had fallen in. Mayor Acornby’s hat, for once, sat quite straight.
